Our discussion above has just begun to scratch the surface of WLAN and RAN scheduling. Additional scheduling disciplines, the provision of qualityof-service guarantees through the hard or soft reservation of resources [Prasad 2023], priority scheduling, scheduling for real-time traffic, and virtualized scheduling [Peterson 2024] are all additionally important topics in this area.

##### 7.3.6 Energy Considerations: Wake/Sleep

Energy is a precious resource in wireless mobile devices, and thus many wireless networks provide explicit power-management capabilities that allow devices to minimize the amount of time that their sense, transmit, and receive functions and other circuitry need to be “on.” To accomplish this, a device will typically alternate between sleep and wake states (not unlike a sleepy student in a classroom!)—waking when there is work to do and sleeping when there is no work to be done. Measurements have shown that an LTE radio can consume between 1,000 and 3, 500 mW of energy while transmitting or receiving (or waiting to receive), but less than 15 mW when powered off—approximately one percent of on-state energy use [Huang 2012]. Measurements have also shown that between 20% to more than 50% of energy use in 4G and 5G devices running popular applications is expended on communication [Xu 2020]. Thus, communication-related energy use plays a central role in overall mobile device energy management.

We can identify two main approaches towards energy management via radio sleep/wake cycles:

• In coordinated sleep/wake approaches, a protocol between the device and the base station serves to coordinate the device’s sleep/wake cycles, with both sides being aware of the device’s sleep/wake state, and the time at which the device is scheduled to awaken next. With this knowledge, the base station can queue arriving datagrams that are destined for the sleeping device, and then transmit these datagrams to the device when it awakens. Both WiFi and 5G networks adopt a coordinated sleep/wake approach.

• In uncoordinated, wake-and-send approaches, a device awakes only when it has data to send. This might happen for example in an IoT device, where an occasional sensor reading is to be transmitted to a logging server via a base station. After waking and transmitting, the device may then wait for messages transmitted to it by the base station in reply, and then return to sleep until the next sensor reading needs to be transmitted. Bluetooth (Section 7.5.1), LoRaWAN (see Section 7.5.3), and 4G LTE Narrowband IoT (NB-IoT) networks adopt an uncoordinated, wake-and-send approach.

Coordinated sleep/wake in IEEE 802.11 networks

802.11 networks have featured power-management capabilities since their inception. A WiFi device indicates to the access point that it will be going to sleep by setting the power-management bit in the header of an 802.11 frame (see Figure 7.26) to 1. Since the AP knows from the set power-transmission bit that the device is going to sleep, the AP will buffer any arriving frames that are destined for the sleeping device until that device awakens.

When the WiFi device wakes up, it will scan for a beacon frame from the AP that contains a Traffic Indication Map (TIM), indicating those devices that have frames that are buffered at the AP and awaiting transmission to that sleeping device. If there are no buffered frames for the device, it can go back to sleep. Otherwise, the device will send polling request messages to the AP, to ask the AP to transmit the buffered frames.

A number of more recent power-management capabilities have also been added to 802.11.WiFi 6 introduced a Target Wake Time (TWT) that allows a device to negotiate the length of its sleep period with the AP. This is valuable in IoT settings where devices may only occasionally report sensor values. The maximum TWT value is 4 years, 5 months, 16 days, 13 hours, 37 minutes, and

39.49 seconds—a very long sleep! The IEEE 802.11ah standard, designed specifically for IoT applications (see Section 7.5.3), inherited IEEE 802.11’s power-saving capabilities and added other enhancements, such as reduced header sizes, to save additional energy. A thorough and readable overview of WiFi’s modern energy-saving mechanisms is [Guerin 2023].

Coordinated sleep/wake in 5G networks As in the case of WiFi, when a user device has nothing to send or receive, there is no reason for its radio to be continuously “on.” Thus, user devices in 5G networks, like their WiFi counterparts, can also go through sleep/wake cycles.

There are two different forms of 5G device sleep/wake cycles, roughly corresponding to a light sleep (perhaps akin to a short “nap”), and a deeper sleep.

Figure 7.38 shows the structure of the light sleep cycle, known as Discontinuous Reception (DRX) in the Connected State. Here, there are two phases ated with powering up the radio, checking for pending downlink transmissions, and powering down the radio. In the example in Figure 7.38, a user device receives a transmission from the base station at t and starts an activity timer. At t , with the device having 0 1 neither received any transmissions since t nor having any transmissions to 0 send, the activity timer expires, and the device enters a short DRX sleep cycle. At the end of each short DRX cycle, the device awakens and checks whether the base station is advertising pending transmissions to it, or whether it has transmissions of its own to send. In this example, since there is no activity for this device over several short sleep cycles, the device then enters a long DRX sleep cycle at t . The device again wakes up at the end of each longer sleep 2 cycle to check for incoming or outgoing transmissions. At t , a packet arrives at 3 the base station for transmission to this device and is buffered, since the device is sleeping. At the end of the long sleep cycle ending at t , the device awakens, 4 finds that the base station is advertising a transmission for the device, enters the active state, eventually receives a transmission from the base station at t , 5 and restarts its inactivity timer. In this example, the increase in latency experienced by the arriving packet due to device sleep is equal to t –t . 5 3 There are additional user device sleep states that are even longer and deeper than the DRX cycles shown in Figure 7.38. After even longer periods of inactivity, a device can enter the Idle state or Inactive state, where it must take additional steps to re-establish its active presence in the RAN before it can send or receive user data. See [Hailu 2019; Developedia 2021; Sauter 2021] for more details. Uncoordinated, wake-and-send in LoRaWAN LoRa (see Section 7.5.3) [Sematech 2019a, 2019b; Sinha 2017] is a low-power, low-bitrate, wireless networking technology for relatively simple IoT devices

Figure 7.38 A user device’s light sleep cycle, with short and long DRX cycles of this light sleep: short DRX cycles and long DRX cycles. The two phases differ, as their names would suggest, only on the length of the sleep period, trading latency (delay until the device receives datagrams that have arrived at the base station destined for the device) with the energy expenditures associ-

![](media/page-543-img-01.png)

Figure 7.39 LoRa wake-and-send whose typical task is to report sensor measurement data to a nearby gateway, typically within a few kilometers of the device. The simplest type of LoRa device, known as a Class A device, uses its radio in an uncoordinated, wakeand-send approach to do so. A device with data to send simply wakes up, transmits its data without any coordination with a gateway node (or even knowing that a gateway node is present), optionally waits for downlink data from the gateway node, and then goes back to sleep. Here, device-energy conservation is a first-class consideration, with the device’s usual sleep state only occasionally disturbed by device-initiated wake-up for data transmission.

![](media/page-544-img-01.png)

Figure 7.39 shows LoRa’s wake-and-send behavior. At t , the LoRa IoT 0 device awakes and sends a LoRa frame (e.g., containing a sensor measurement) to the LoRa gateway. The device then looks for messages from the gateway, and receiving none, returns to sleep at t . At t , the gateway has a 1 2 message to send to the IoT device but must wait until the next device contact (following t ) before sending the message. The gateway’s message is received 3 at t and the device returns to sleep at t . 4 5 Like LoRa Class A, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) and 4G LTE Narrowband IoT (NB-IoT) networks also support device-initiated wake-and-send transmission by the IoT device. However, in these cases, the device must first contact the controller node or base station upon waking to first be allocated channel transmission slots in which to send its data. See [Sauter 2021] for details.

#### 7.4 The Wireless Core Network

Having learned about wireless access networks in Section 7.3, we’ll now move from the wireless edge and into the wireless core. The 5G Core provides higher-level control-plane and management-plane services (e.g., for managing user-device identity, access security, mobility, and more) as well as the dataplane services to forward datagrams between devices in the 5G RAN and the larger Internet.

In this section we’ll focus entirely on 5G networks rather than covering both 5G and WiFi networks. Indeed, there is no reason to discuss core control and management for WiFi networks here, since traditional IP networks use the same management and control-plane mechanisms for both wired Ethernet and WiFi. An enterprise views WiFi, or any wireless edge network, as just another link-layer technology in its network.

One might wonder why the core network is such a central architectural component in mobile cellular networks, but not in traditional IP networks. The answer undoubtedly lies in 5G’s roots in mobile cellular telephony. 1G and 2G cellular networks were essentially telephone-only networks; 3G networks were still primarily telephone networks, with packet data grafted on as an additional service. These early cellular networks supported services for managing user identity (e.g., via SIM cards); device mobility within a provider’s network; roaming among different provider networks; and accounting, billing, payment and settlement for services. There was no support for such services in the deployed Internet at the time. 4G and 5G networks have now become “all IP” networks and have adopted many of the services pioneered in traditional IP networks. Nonetheless, native support for services such as identity, mobility, roaming and service billing—services implemented primarily in the 5G Core—is not implemented in traditional Internet ISPs, and remains a significant difference between 4G 5G networks and traditional IP networks today.

In this section, we’ll provide an overview of the 5G Core and its services in Section 7.4.1. We’ll focus on the User Plane network function and the extensive use of tunneling in Section 7.4.2 and then cover user identity and its role in registration and session establishment in Section 7.4.3. Mobility is such an important topic that we’ll give this a separate treatment in Section 7.5.

##### 7.4.1 The 5G Core and Network Functions

Figure 7.40, adapted from [3GPP 23.501 2024], shows a number of the key 5G Core components. The 5G Core adopts a Service-Based Architecture (SBA), with architectural elements in the Core defined in terms of Network Functions (NFs) and the services they provide. Although the 5G specifications do not specify how these functions are to be implemented, a service-based description would naturally map (as suggested by various figures in this chapter) onto microservices implemented in a logically centralized data center. This approach differs significantly from 4G and earlier cellular network architectures that defined traditional network “entities” that interacted via protocols and were typically implemented by standalone single-function equipment (“boxes”).

Perhaps reflecting this break from 4G, 5G service elements have completely new names and abbreviations than their 4G counterparts, causing occasional headaches for students learning about cellular networks who can be overwhelmed by names and acronyms in the cellular network world.

Many of the innovations in the 5G Core—in particular the evolution from “boxes” to “services,” the opportunity for SDN-based implementation of services, and the clear separation between the control plane and user plane—mirror the earlier evolution of the Internet control plane that we learned about in Chapter 5.

Figure 7.40 5G Core: key network functions

![](media/page-546-img-01.png)

5G Network Functions If one were to identify the “top three” most centrally important Network Func- tions in the 5G Core, these three functions would be leading candidates: • The User Plane Function (UPF) is responsible for the data-plane for- warding of traffic between the RAN and the larger Internet.

As the only 5G network function in the data plane, it clearly plays a central role. As we’ll see in Section 7.4.2, the User Plane Function is structured as a tun- neled relay that forwards user IP datagrams between the base station and the larger Internet. Every datagram transmitted by a device to the larger Internet and vice versa will pass through the device’s User Plane Function. • The Access, Mobility Management Function (AMF) plays the key role in authorizing and establishing device access to a 5G network’s services and in managing device mobility (discussed in Section 7.5). The AMF is arguably the central Network Function in the 5G control plane. As we will see, the AMF works with many other network functions to implement its services. For example, the AMF interacts with the Authentication Server Function (AUSF) to authenticate a device that wants to join a 5G network. The AMF is also the only control-plane network function that exchanges control messages directly with a device, via the N1 interface shown in Figure 7.40, and is one of only two network functions that directly exchange control messages with a base station (via the N2 interface). A numbered interface such as N1 is known as a reference point in 3GPP parlance and defines the interaction between a 5G core function and another Core function (or device or base station). [3GPP 23.501 2024] standardizes more than 60 such reference points.

• The Session Management Function (SMF) manages each device session, including IP address allocation and assignment (e.g., NAT and DHCP-like services) and the installation of per-device state for functions such as policy-based access control, charging, and establishing device data-plane forwarding via the UPF.

Network, user, and application data and state information also figure prominently in the set of network functions. Device profile, service and authentication information is managed by the Unified Data Management (UDM) Network Function. The UDM may store its data internally within its function implementation or externally in the Unified Data Repository (UDR).

When a Network Function chooses to store data externally in the Unified Data Repository and accesses and updates this information remotely, stateless transactions (similar in spirit to the stateless client/server interaction in HTTP) are possible, naturally leading to scalable and resilient network function implementations in a cloud environment. Other network functions and third-party applications can also store and retrieve data to and from the Unified Data Repository and the Unstructured Data Storage Function (UDSF).

In Section 7.3.3, we learned that user application code can run on servers in the 5G Core or at the base station and communicate with devices to implement an application’s service, a capability known as local breakout. The Network Exposure Function (NEF) and Application Function (AF) expose select network data and Network Function services to these local-breakout applications, and vice versa.

Sometimes a Network Function running in one operator’s 5G network will need to interact with a counterpart in another operator’s 5G network. For example, when your smartphone wants to join a network not operated by the network provider with whom you have a paid subscription plan (known as your “home” network), the Authentication Server Function (AUSF) in the network that you want to join will interact with its peer AUSF in your home network to perform authentication and to determine the set of services available to you. The authentication functions in these two networks will securely communicate with each other via their local Security Edge Protection Proxy (SEPP) Network Function.

Finally, capabilities are needed for network functions to register their services and discover the potentially large number of other network functions. The Network Repository Function (NRF) provides these automatic registration and discovery services, obviating the need for complex manual configuration. The Policy Control Function (PCF) provides control, management, and centralized repository services for control policy rules used for mobility management, per-device quality of service, and roaming. One important new concept introduced in 5G is network slicing, which involves the virtualization of RAN and Core resources, and the ability to define multiple logical networks that share the network’s underlying physical resources, in much the same way that we learned (in Section 6.5) that multiple virtual private networks (VPNs) can operate over the same set of physical network resources in traditional IP networks. The Network Slice Selection Function (NSSF) is the network function that plays the central role in network slicing, a topic beyond the scope of this book.

As we will see, a network function will typically interact with other network functions to implement its service. Network functions can communicate with each other using several different styles of interaction, and the standards do not mandate or recommend one approach over another. NF services may be accessed using the traditional request/response client-server model that we studied in Chapter 2, which in turn can be implemented via a protocol such as HTTP, or by remote procedure calls in a data center setting. Another form of client-server interaction is the subscribe/notify model (aka the publish/ subscribe model in the distributed systems literature) in which a client registers its interest in a service, and the server notifies the client when results from the service are available (i.e., “pushes” results to subscribed clients).

Recall that we learned in Chapter 5 that the publish/subscribe model is the central organizing principle in Google’s Orion SDN platform.

##### 7.4.2 User Plane Function

We learned above that the User Plane Function is responsible for controlling the data-plane forwarding of traffic between the RAN and the larger Internet. Since the 5G data plane is an all-IP network, in many ways it functions exactly as we’ve already seen in Chapters 4 and 5.However, the 5G control plane configures the data plane to support two key services not always found in traditional IP networks: quality of service (QoS) support and tunneling. 5G QoS support is an advanced topic beyond the scope of this book; see [Sauter 2021] for a discussion.

In this subsection, we’ll consider tunneling together with the protocol stacks in the 5G data plane that implement tunneling.

Recall from Chapters 4 and 6 that tunneling provides the abstraction of a virtual link between two IP devices. In a 5G setting, a tunnel is established for each device between its base station and its instance of the User Plane Function, as shown in Figure 7.41. With tunneling, the entire sea of routers and links in the backhaul network between the base station and the User Plane Function is abstracted as a single virtual link for that device.

Having studied the RAN protocol stacks in detail in Section 7.3, let’s now focus on the data-plane protocol stacks at the base station and the User Plane Function in the 5G Core. As discussed in Section 7.4.3, the Session Management Function will establish a tunnel between the base station and the device’s User Plane Function when a device joins the network. When a User Plane Function receives a datagram from the external Internet that is destined for a device in its data plane, the User Plane Function encapsulates that datagram within a UDP segment using the GPRS Tunneling Protocol (GTP) [3GPP TS

29.281 2022]. The UDP datagram then becomes the payload in a new IP datagram, which is forwarded from the User Plane Function through the backhaul network to the base station, just like any other IP datagram addressed to the base station. On the receiving side, the base station decapsulates the tunneled UDP datagram from the User Plane Function, extracts the encapsulated IP within-a-datagram in Figure 7.41. The protocol details of the tunneling protocol are fairly straightforward and can be found in [3GPP TS 29.281 2022]. So rather than diving into those details here, let’s instead consider the more fundamental question of why tunneling is used in the first place. In Chapter 4, we learned that tunneling allowed IPv4 and IPv6 networks to interoperate. But what are the advantages to wrapping a datagram inside a datagram while operating in a pure 5G network? The answer lies in device mobility, i.e., a device changing the base station to which it is attached (Section 7.4) as it moves through the cellular provider’s network. Consider again the example in Figure 7.41. Without tunneling, all of the routers in the backhaul network would need to maintain up-to-date information about a device’s location (i.e., the base station to which the device is currently attached) in order to forward a datagram to that device. Indeed, the routers would need to maintain that information for all devices in the provider’s network! With tunneling, only the tunnel endpoint (i.e., the User Plane Function) needs to know the identity of the base station to which the device is attached; the backhaul routers need only know how to forward and route datagrams to and from the base stations. The UPF thus serves as an anchor point for forwarding datagrams from a device to the larger Internet, and vice versa, for the

Figure 7.41 5G protocol stacks, with tunneling datagram destined for the device, and forwards that IP datagram over the RAN to the device. As with the use of tunneling in mixed IPv4 v6 networks (Section 4.3), you should carefully examine the addresses in the datagram-

![](media/page-549-img-01.png)

duration of a device’s attachment to the 5G network, regardless of the particular base station to which the device happens to be attached at a given time.

##### 7.4.3 User Identity, Registration, and Session Establishment

In Section 7.3.4, we learned how a device discovers the existence of a 5G network and how it initially attaches to a base station. Recall that following this initial attachment, although the device and base station are able to exchange control messages, the device still has not yet really joined the 5G network—it hasn’t yet exchanged control messages with the 5G Core and so can’t yet, for example, send or receive data-plane datagrams via a User Plane Function.

Let’s begin our discussion of how a device fully joins a 5G network by first considering how the device identifies itself to the network.

Identity: SIM Cards As most cell phone owners know, a 4G 5G device needs a physical SIM (Subscriber Identity Module) card, or more recently a software-only eSIM, to attach to a 4G 5G network. Your SIM uniquely identifies you and your “home” network to all cellular network providers globally. In the cellular network world, your SIM is your global network identity!

The information included in a SIM can differ from one provider to another, but will generally include the following information:

• IMSI: International Mobile Subscriber Identity. An IMSI has three parts:

a 3-digit (base 10) mobile country code (MCC), a 2- or 3-digit mobile network code (MNC) and a mobile subscription identification number (MSIN).The MCC and MNC together define the SIM’s home network, i.e., the cellular provider that provided the SIM card to you and with whom you have a subscription plan. The MSIN uniquely identifies the SIM within the home network. Your SIM also has your cellular phone number and an associated set of cellular services that you’re able to access when attached to your home network.

When you’re in an area not served by your home network, you may attach to another provider’s network, in which case you are said to be roaming on a visited network. You may have a different set of services available to you on visited networks, depending on your subscription plan with your home network and the charging/settlement mechanisms between your home network and the visited network. There may be networks that, with great frustration, you simply cannot join.

• Cryptographic keys and PINs are also stored on a SIM. The cryptographic key is used for authenticating the device when it joins the 5G network, as discussed below and in Chapter 8.

• Local Area Identity information lists current and recently visited networks. Local identity is used to identify networks that a device may try first when seeking cellular network service.

• Contact lists and text messages may also be stored on a SIM card.

Joining a 5G network: registration and session establishment When a device wants to join a 5G network, there are two important sets of actions that are undertaken. The first is registration, when the device identifies and then authenticates itself to the network, and vice versa. The second is PDU Session establishment, which allocates an IP address for the device and creates a data-plane path between the device and a User Plane Function. “PDU” is an acronym for “Protocol Data Unit”—3GPP jargon for a “packet.” After these steps, the device is fully attached to the network, and ready to go (communicate while being mobile)!

Both registration and session establishment are performed by network functions in the 5G Core, with Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF) playing a central role in this process. The AMF is the only Network Function that communicates directly with the base station and the device. It orchestrates authentication (with the AUSF) and session establishment (with the SMF) within the 5G Core.

Let’s now briefly consider the steps involved in registration and session establishment, as shown in Figure 7.42.

Figure 7.42 Device registration and session establishment: interaction among device, base

station and Core Network Functions

![](media/page-551-img-01.png)

• Registration. Earlier in Section 7.3.4, we learned that the device and base station exchange connection setup request/response messages to establish a RAN signaling channel between themselves. After this exchange, the base station then selects an instance of the AMF for the device and sends a registration request to that AMF for that device. The AMF then contacts the device and requests and receives device identity information. As shown in Figure 7.42, that information is then passed to the Authentication Function which performs mutual authentication with the device; we’ll postpone our discussion of 5G authentication until Chapter 8, where we’ll cover this topic in detail. Note that if the network being joined by the device is not its home network, the local Authentication Function in the visited network will serve as a proxy to the Authentication Function in the device’s home network, which will actually perform the authentication. Following a successful authentication, the AMF then registers the device’s identity and subscribed service information in the local UDM, and returns a registration acceptance message to the device.

• Session establishment. The device initiates the process that will establish its data plane by sending a PDU session establishment request to the AMF, which in turn selects an SMF that will be responsible for establishing and managing the device’s data plane, while the device is attached to the network. After verifying via the User Data Management Function that the device’s requested session parameters are permissible, the SMF selects an instance of the User Plane Function and establishes the device’s tunnel between its base station and that User Plane Function. The SMF then returns the tunnel, IPv4 address information, and additional session information to the device via the AMF and the base station. The final step is for the base station and the device to interact to configure the device’s RAN data plane. Once this is done, the device is then ready to send datagrams into the Internet!

In the above, we’ve illustrated only the most important interactions among the device, base station, and various network functions in registration and session establishment. We note that the Policy Control Function and the Charging Function are also involved in session establishment and that additional steps are needed to configure IPv6, if desired. For a full discussion of the process, see [3GPP TS 23.502 2024], and the discussion (34 rather dense pages!) surrounding Figures 4.2.2.2.2-1 and 4.3.2.2.1.

#### 7.5 Mobility

Having covered the characteristics of wireless links and the physical layer of wireless networks in Section 7.2, wireless access networks in Section 7.3 and wireless core networks in Section 7.4, let’s now turn our attention to one of the most unique and interesting aspects of wireless networks—the need to support device mobility. Indeed, this topic is so important that we are devoting an entire section to the topic! We’ll begin in Section 7.5.1 by discussing the challenges introduced by the need to support mobile devices and the principles and broad approaches towards doing so. While WiFi naturally supports mobility in the vicinity of an access point, we’ll see that WiFi (Section 7.5.2) only provides limited support for mobility among nearby WiFi WLANs. By contrast, cellular networks have had mobility “baked in” as a first-class, “must-have” service since their earliest days due to their roots in the mobile telephony world. We’ll cover the extensive support for mobility in 5G networks in Section 7.5.3.

In Section 7.5.4, we’ll wrap our discussion of mobility with observations about past IETF efforts for supporting network-layer mobility within and among non-cellular IP networks, and possibly why such mobile Internet service has not been deployed to date.

##### 7.5.1 Mobility Principles

What is “mobility”?

Let’s begin our discussion of device mobility by carefully considering what we mean by “mobility” in the first place. Suppose a device is “on” and communicating as it moves, and let’s consider how “far” such a device can move while communicating without interruption (e.g., maintaining ongoing TCP connections and not needing to explicitly join any new networks). Drawing on the distinction made between inter-domain and intra-domain routing, we can identify three distinct mobility scenarios, depending on whether or not a device is able to move without interrupting ongoing communication within and among access networks (e.g., 802.11 WLANs or 5G RANs) with a single provider’s network, and within and among the multiple provider networks.

• Mobility only within a single access network. At one end of the spectrum, scenario (a) in Figure 7.43, a mobile device maintains its communication connectivity only while attached to a given access network.

In this scenario, a device must disconnect from the base station in one access network, and then connect to a new base station in another access network, as it moves between access networks. For example, a student might disconnect from a wireless classroom network and power down their laptop or smartphone, head to the dining commons and connect to the wireless access network there while eating, and then disconnect and power down from the dining commons network, walk to the library, and connect to the library’s wireless network while studying. In this case, the device serially associates with (joins), and later disassociates from (leaves), each wireless access network encountered. This case of limited device mobility can be completely handled using the networking mechanisms we’ve already studied in Sections 7.3 and 7.4.

• Mobility among access networks within a single provider network. Our interest in device mobility really starts with case (b), where a device moves among multiple access networks within a provider’s network while continuing to send and receive IP datagrams, and while maintaining higherlevel (e.g., TCP) connections. Here, the network will need to provide handover—a transfer of responsibility for forwarding datagrams to/ from one base station to another as the device moves among WLANs or

Figure 7.43 Various degrees of mobility, as a device maintains connectivity

![](media/page-554-img-01.png)

RANs. When handover occurs within access networks belonging to a single network provider, that single provider’s network orchestrates handover on its own. • Mobility among multiple network providers. When a mobile device roams between multiple provider networks, as in scenario (c) in Figure 7.43, the providers must coordinate handover to ensure uninterrupted ongoing communication. This inter-provider handoff significantly complicates the process. As scenario (c) is more complex and occurs less often as cellular network providers increase their geographical footprints, we’ll focus our attention here on case (b). See Chapter 7 in earlier editions of this book, available on our pub- lisher’s and authors’ Web sites, for a discussion of scenario (c). Mobility: challenges and approaches Any approach toward supporting device mobility among access networks within a single provider network (case (b) in Figure 7.43) must consider three fundamental questions: • Is device mobility supported only at the link layer, or is the network layer involved as well? If mobility is supported only at the link layer, a device may be able to move among wireless access (link-layer) networks, but this may restrict a device’s mobility range while communicating without interruption to be within its current subnet (in the addressing sense of Section 4.3). This is because, with only link-layer mobility support, incoming datagrams from the larger Internet that are destined to the device will always be forwarded to this subnet for delivery to the device. As we will see in Section 7.5.3, this is the approach taken in enterprise WiFi networks. • On the other hand, if device mobility is supported across the provider’s entire network, network-layer (and/or higher-layer) support will be needed. For example, the core network will need to know the particular access network to which the mobile device is currently attached, so that incoming datagrams from the larger Internet can be forwarded to that subnet for delivery to the device. As we will see in Section 7.5.3, this is the approach taken in 5G (and 3G and 4G) cellular networks.

• Why is handover initiated, and who initiates handover? When a device changes its point of attachment to the network from one base station to another, why is that change made in the first place? As we saw in Section 7.2, as a device moves, the quality of the radio signal between itself and the base station (and hence packet throughput and latency) can change. A device might thus change access networks to improve its performance. However, the network itself may choose to move the device from one access network to another in order to load-balance devices among its access networks. The WiFi and 5G standards do not specify specific algorithms to be used by a base station to determine whether or not to perform handover, or which target base station to choose. That decision is left up to network operators and remains an active area of research [Haghrah 2023].

• A wireless device will also typically measure the signal quality of all base stations within range and report that information back to the base station to which it is currently attached. We learned in Section 7.3.5 that in 5G networks, a base station periodically broadcasts reference signal symbols and that a device periodically reports a 4-bit channel quality indication (CQI) to the base station based on its measured reception of these reference signals. WiFi devices measure the strength of the signal received from various APs and return a Received Signal Strength Indicator for each of these APs. These measured and reported values can then be used to decide whether a device should be handed over to a different base station. A device or network could also predict future device mobility and radio signal strength (e.g., using machine learning) and proactively perform handover, rather than relying just on current measurements. The decision to perform a handover may be initiated and controlled primarily by the device, or by the control plane in the network’s base stations.

• How is handoff accomplished? When a device that is associated with one base station is handed off to another base station, two important tasks must be accomplished. First, device state (e.g., the authenticated status of the device, the device’s allowed services) within the WLAN or RAN control plane in one base station must be transferred to the neighboring base station. Without this transfer, a device would have to disassociate from the old base station, and associate with the new base station. Secondly, to ensure the uninterrupted bi-directional flow of datagrams to and from the mobile device, forwarding tables in routers and switches must be modified to redirect datagrams to and from the device when there is a new point of attachment to the network.

In the following two subsections, we’ll study how these mobility considerations are addressed in institutional WiFi networks (Section 7.5.3) and 5G cellular networks (Section 7.5.4).

##### 7.5.2 Mobility in a WiFi network

The IEEE 802.11 WiFi standard adopts a decidedly link-layer-only approach towards mobility, perhaps not surprising because 802.11 is a link-layer standard. Consequently, WiFi mobility is supported only among access points that are within the same subnet (in the addressing sense of Section 4.3).

![](media/page-556-img-01.png)

Figure 7.44 WiFi: handover within the ESS

We learned in Section 7.3.2 (Figure 7.22) that the traditional WiFi network, known as the Basic Service Set (BSS), contains a single AP and one or more attached wireless devices. Figure 7.44 shows the concept of an Extended Service Set (ESS), which consists of multiple BSSs (e.g., BSS and BSS ) and their 2 3 set of access points (e.g., AP and AP in Figure 7.44). Assuming that each AP 2 3 in the ESS uses the same SSID, an ESS appears logically to be just a single WLAN from both the device point of view and from the network-layer point of view, since the devices and APs in the ESS are in the same layer-3 subnet. Indeed, a device that moves between BSS and BSS in Figure 7.44 is not even mobile 2 3 from a network-layer point of view, since it never leaves its subnet! The IEEE 802.11 standard introduced Fast Basic Service Set Transition (FT) to accelerate  the  802.1X authentication when a device moves between APs in an ESS, and to allow APs to suggest alternative APs to which a device may wish to attach within the ESS.

In addition to these 802.11 standard capabilities, large WiFi equipment vendors provide proprietary solutions that provide support for mobility, e.g., to manage device handover between two APs in an ESS [Cisco 802.11r 2016].

##### 7.5.3 Mobility in a 5G network

While 802.11 mobility occurs exclusively at the link layer, mobility in a cellular 5G network is a network-wide undertaking, involving both RANs and the 5G Core network. 5G’s extensive support for device mobility undoubtedly reflects its roots in the mobile cellular telephony world. The earliest generations of cellular networks provided call handover with uninterrupted voice service as a user ranged from cell to cell across a provider’s network, as well as from one provider’s network to another. With mobility “baked in” to the earliest cellular network architectures, the addition of mobile data services followed quite naturally in later generation cellular networks.

In this subsection, we’ll focus on the handover process in 5G networks. As we’ll see, handover is carefully orchestrated within the RAN and 5G Core control planes, and also involves the reconfiguration of the device’s RAN and 5G Core data planes, making it a truly network-wide activity.

5G Handover Let’s consider an active 5G device that is currently associated with a base station in one RAN (the “source” base station for the handover) that will be handed over to a second base station (the “target” base station) in another RAN.Let’s suppose that the device is “active” in the sense that it has an ongoing TCP connection with a remote host in the larger Internet and an active data-plane connection via a tunnel to/from its User Plane Function in the Core (see Section 7.4.2).

After handover, the device will be associated with the target base station, the source base station will have released the device state it had been maintaining, the data-plane tunnel to and from the device will now end in the second RAN (assuming for simplicity that the other tunnel endpoint remains at the same User Plane Function), and all device states in the 5G Core will reflect the fact that the device is now located in the newly-joined base station. So many changes that will need to be made!

Figure 7.45, adapted from Figures 4.9.1.2.2-1 in [3GPP TS 23.502 2024] and 9.2.3.2.1-1 in [3GPP TS 38.300 2024], illustrates the handover process. 5G handover begins in the RANs, and then completes in the Core. Most of the handover interactions shown in Figure 7.45 are in the control plane, but the data-plane tunnel between the User Plane Function and the base station to which the user is associated will also change during the process. We can identify three distinct phases in 5G handover:

• Making the handover decision. Handover begins in the RAN, with the device measuring the quality of the radio channels of the base stations that it can hear, and then reporting these measurements to the source base station. If a handover is deemed desirable by the source base station, it sends a handover request message to the target base station, which then decides whether or not to accept the handover and returns its decision (in the case of the example in Figure 7.45, a positive acknowledgment) to the source base station.

• Transferring the device between base stations. The source base station, target base station and the device then work together to transfer the device’s RAN connection from the source base station to the target base station.

This process begins with the source base station sending two messages: a reconfiguration message to the device and a transfer status message to the target base station that transfers device state to the target base station. The device and the target base station can then set up a new RAN connection.

The process completes when the device sends a reconfiguration complete message to the target base station and the target and source base stations perform a final handshake. Note that the endpoint of the tunnel between the base station and the User Plane Function remains unchanged during this process. However, rather than delivering datagrams to the device over the source RAN, the source base station instead begins forwarding datagrams addressed to the device to the target base station. The target the handover process. • Updating device state and UPF tunnel in the Core. Handover activity now shifts to the Core. The target base station, which is now fully in charge of the device’s RAN connection, signals to the Session Management Func- tion (SMF) via the AMF that it is the new base station for the device being handed over. The SMF then signals to the User Plane Function to change the device’s tunnel to be terminated at the target base station. The User Plane Function then sends a data-end marker to the source base station, which then knows that the device tunnel endpoint has been switched and informs the target base station. At this point, the target base station can deliver to the device any buffered datagrams forwarded to it from the source base station during handover. Additionally, datagrams will now flow directly from the device’s User Plane Function to the target base station. Following some cleanup handshaking, the handover process is now complete!

Figure 7.45 Device handover: RAN and Core actions base station will buffer these datagrams for later delivery to the device, ensuring that no incoming datagrams destined for the device are lost in

![](media/page-558-img-01.png)

While our description above might seem rather complicated, it actually only considers the simplest of handover scenarios! One common scenario not covered above is the case in which a device has powered off its radio to conserve power. Recall from Section 7.3 that after periods of inactivity, there are sleep periods that are even longer than the DRX sleep cycles we encountered in Figure 7.38. During these periods of long sleep, a device will first enter the Idle state and then the Inactive state. In the Idle state, a device must take additional steps to re-establish its active presence in the RAN before it can send or receive user data. In the Inactive state, additional handover steps must be taken in both the RAN and in the Core. In particular, if a device moves among base stations while Idle or Inactive, the 5G Core may not even know the RAN in which the device is located. Tracking area update procedures can be used so that the Core knows the general area where the device is located. Paging procedures can then be used by the Core to pinpoint the device’s RAN. These topics are beyond the scope of our discussion here; see [Alsaeedy 2019] for a discussion.

A more complex handover also occurs when a device is handed over from the RAN in one provider’s mobile cellular network to the RAN in another provider’s network. In this case, the cellular provider to which the device is attached changes and inter-provider signaling is needed; see [3GPP TS 138.300 2024] for details.

##### 7.5.4 Internet Mobility

Today’s traditional (non-cellular) Internet does not have any widely deployed infrastructure that provides the type of services for “on the go” mobile users that we encountered for 5G cellular networks.

This, however, is not due to the lack of technical solutions for providing such services! Indeed, a Mobile IP architecture and protocols [RFC 5944] were standardized in Internet RFCs more than 25 years ago. Interested readers can consult earlier editions of our book and [Perkins 1998] for an in-depth treatment of Mobile IP. And research has continued on new, more secure and more generalized Internet mobility solutions [Venkataramani 2014].

Given Mobile IP’s technical solutions, it has perhaps been the lack of motivating business and use cases [Arkko 2012] and the timely, first-mover development and deployment of alternative mobility solutions in cellular networks that blunted the deployment of Mobile IP. Recall that 25 years ago, 3G cellular networks had already provided a solution for mobile voice services (the “killer app” for mobile users) as well as the beginnings of global mobile data services. Behind these services was a paid subscription model with a home network provider, and inter-provider business agreements and payments that allowed users to roam from their home networks to visited networks. The traditional Internet lacks such a business infrastructure in support of roaming.

Today, mobile Internet connectivity is provided via a dual technology solution—mobile services via cellular networks when we are truly mobile and “on the go” (i.e., the center and rightmost side of the mobility spectrum in Figure 7.44) and Internet services via 802.11 networks or wireline networks when we are stationary or moving locally (i.e., the center and leftmost side of the mobility spectrum in Figure 7.44). Perhaps this dual-technology solution that we’ve now had in place for 25 years will continue to persist into the future.

The one indisputable fact however, is that 15 years ago there were approximately equal numbers of subscribers attached to the Internet via fixed (wired) broadband technologies and via wireless technologies. While both subscriber bases have grown since then, there are now five times as many Internetconnected wireless subscribers than wired subscribers. There’s a saying that customers “vote with their feet.” That may be a particularly apt description of the choices that highly mobile Internet users have made.

#### 7.6 Bluetooth, Satellite, and IoT Wireless Networks

In the past three sections, we’ve focused primarily on WiFi and 5G networks.

But these are not the only types of widely deployed wireless networks! In this section, we’ll thus briefly cover three additional types of wireless networks— Bluetooth, satellite, and IoT wireless networks. As we’ll see, because these networks provide more specialized services than WiFi and 5G networks, they have interestingly different architectures and protocols.

##### 7.6.1 Bluetooth networks

Bluetooth networks have quickly become part of everyday life. You may have used a Bluetooth network as a cable-replacement technology to interconnect a computer with a wireless keyboard, mouse, or other peripheral device. Or perhaps you’ve used a Bluetooth network to connect wireless earbuds, speaker, watch, or health monitoring band to a smartphone or to connect a smartphone to a car’s audio system. In all of these cases, Bluetooth operates over short ranges (tens of meters or less), at low power, and at low cost. For this reason, Bluetooth networks are sometimes referred to as wireless personal area networks  (WPANs) or, because of their limited range, piconets.

Although Bluetooth networks are small and relatively simple by design, they’re packed with many of the link-level networking techniques that we’ve studied earlier, including time division and frequency division multiplexing (Section 6.3.1), randomized backoff (Section 6.3.2), polling (Section 6.3.3), error detection and correction (Section 6.2), and reliable data transfer and flow control (Chapter 3). And that’s just considering Bluetooth’s link layer!

Bluetooth networks operate in the unlicensed 2.4 GHz Industrial, Scientific, and Medical (ISM) radio band along with other home appliances such as microwaves, garage door openers, and cordless phones. As a result, Bluetooth networks are designed explicitly with noise and interference in mind. The Bluetooth wireless channel is operated in a combined TDM and FDM manner, with 79 frequency channels and 625 microsecond time slots on each channel.

During each time slot, a sender transmits on one of the 79 channels. The sender then changes the channel (frequency) used in a pre-determined manner from one slot to the next, as shown in Figure 7.46.

![](media/page-561-img-01.png)

Figure 7.46 Bluetooth frequency hopping over time

This form of channel hopping, known as frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS), is used so that interference from another device operating at a given frequency in the ISM band will only interfere with Bluetooth communications in a small number of slots. Additionally, slots with significant interference, as manifested in a low signal-to-noise ratio, can be adaptively removed from the hopping pattern. Multiple Bluetooth networks can co-exist in the same physical space as long as they use different frequency hopping patterns. Bluetooth data rates can reach up to 2 to 3 Mbps.

Bluetooth networks are ad hoc networks, as no network infrastructure (i.e., base station) is needed.

In most usage cases, Bluetooth communication is between only two devices, e.g., between wireless earphones and a smartphone.

But the Bluetooth standard also allows for devices to organize themselves into networks, and so a multiple access protocol is required. Bluetooth devices organize themselves into a piconet of up to eight active devices, as shown in Figure 7.47. One of these devices is designated as the centralized controller, with the remaining devices acting as clients in a “peripheral” role. The centralized controller node truly rules the piconet—its clock determines time in the

![](media/page-561-img-02.png)

Figure 7.47 A Bluetooth piconet

piconet (e.g., determines TDM slot boundaries), it determines the slot-to-slot frequency hopping sequence, it controls entry of client devices into the piconet, it controls the power (100 mW, 2.5 mW, or 1 mW) at which peripheral devices transmit, and (using polling) it grants transmission privileges to a peripheral device once it has been admitted to the network.

In Bluetooth, communication occurs only between the central and peripheral nodes; there is no direct peripheral-to-peripheral communication.

Because Bluetooth ad hoc networks must be self-organizing, it’s worth looking into how they bootstrap their network structure. When a centralized controller node wants to form a Bluetooth network, it must first determine which other Bluetooth devices are within range; this is the neighbor-discovery problem. The centralized controller does this by broadcasting a series of 32 inquiry messages, each on a different frequency channel, and repeats the transmission sequence up to 128 times. A client device listens on its chosen frequency, hoping to hear one of the centralized controller’s inquiry messages on this frequency. When it hears an inquiry message, it backs off a random amount of time between 0 and 0.3 seconds (to avoid collisions with other responding nodes, reminiscent of WiFi’s and Ethernet’s binary backoff) and then responds to the centralized controller with a message containing its device ID.

As the Bluetooth centralized controller discovers potential clients within range, it can then invite those clients that it wishes to join its piconet. This second phase is known as Bluetooth paging (not to be confused with paging in 5G networks) and is reminiscent of 802.11 clients associating with a base station.

The centralized controller begins the paging process by again sending 32 identical paging invitation messages, each now addressed to a specific client, but again using different frequencies, since a client doesn’t yet know the frequency-hopping pattern. Once the client replies with an ACK message to the paging invitation message, the centralized controller sends frequency-hopping information, clock synchronization information, and an active member address to the client. It then finally polls the client, now using the frequency-hopping pattern, to ensure that the client is connected into the network.

Because Bluetooth was designed for a specific, limited set of services (unlike the Internet and 5G networks), it’s instructive to take a quick look at its protocol stack, shown in Figure 7.48. Perhaps most strikingly, the Bluetooth protocol stack lacks both a network layer and a traditional transport layer! The lack of a network layer is perhaps not surprising, given that Bluetooth networks are generally single-hop with only controller-to-peripheral, or peripheral-to-controller transmissions, and so multi-hop forwarding and routing are not of concern. Multi-hop extensions of the basic Bluetooth mechanisms do exist in the Bluetooth Scatternet and more recently, the Low Energy Mesh specifications, but these have seen extremely limited deployment [Todtenberg 2019]. Many of the Internet’s end-to-end transport-layer services—including reliable data transfer, flow control, segmentation, connection-oriented and connection-less services and an API for upper-layer applications—are provided in Bluetooth’s Logical Link Control and Adaptation Protocol (L2CAP) layer.

L2CAP also provides a service that reserves periodic slots for a connection’s transmissions; this is useful for multimedia applications with known bandwidth requirements and fixed timings.

Figure 7.48 Bluetooth protocol stack Bluetooth 2025].

![](media/page-563-img-01.png)

In our discussion above, we have only touched on Bluetooth wireless networking. More recent versions of Bluetooth have emphasized low-energy and security considerations. For more information about Bluetooth, the interested reader should consult [Colbach 2017; Todtenberg 2019; Sauter 2021;

Location Discovery GPS and Wifi Positioning Many of the most useful and important smartphone apps today are location-based mobile apps, including Foursquare, Yelp, Uber, Pokémon Go, and Waze. These software apps all make use of an API that allows them to extract their current geographical position directly from the smartphone. Have you ever wondered how your smartphone obtains its geographical position? Today, it is done by combining two systems: the Global Positioning System (GPS) and the WiFi Positioning System (WPS).

The GPS, with a constellation of 30 + satellites, broadcasts satellite location

and timing information, which in turn is used by each GPS receiver to estimate its geolocation. The United States government created the system, maintains it, and makes it freely accessible to anyone with a GPS receiver. The satellites have very stable atomic clocks that are synchronized with one another and with ground clocks. The satellites also know their locations with great precision. Each GPS satellite continuously broadcasts a radio signal containing its current time and position. If a GPS receiver obtains this information from at least four satellites, it can solve trilateration equations to estimate its position.

GPS, however, cannot always provide accurate geolocations if it does not have line-of-sight with at least four GPS satellites or when there is interference from other high-frequency communication systems. This is particularly true in urban environments, where tall buildings frequently block GPS signals. This is where WiFi positioning systems come to the rescue. WiFi positioning systems make use of databases of WiFi access points, which are independently maintained by various Internet companies, including Google, Apple, and Microsoft. Each database contains information about millions of WiFi access points, including each access point’s SSID and an estimate of its geographic location. To understand how a WiFi positioning system makes use of such a database, consider an Android smartphone along with the Google location service. From each nearby access point, the smartphone receives and measures the signal strength of beacon signals (see Section 7.3.4), which contain the access point’s SSID. The smartphone can therefore continually send messages to the Google location service (in the cloud) that include the SSIDs of nearby access points and the corresponding signal strengths. It will also send its GPS position (obtained via the satellite broadcast signals, as described above) when available. Using the signal-strength information, Google will estimate the distance between the smartphone and each of the WiFi access points. Leveraging these estimated distances, it can then solve trilateration equations to estimate the smartphone’s geolocation. Finally, this WiFi-based estimate is combined with the GPS satellite-based estimate to form an aggregate estimate, which is then sent back to the smartphone and used by the location-based mobile apps.

But you may still be wondering how Google (and Apple, Microsoft, and so on) obtain and maintain the database of access points, and in particular, the access point’s geographic location? Recall that for a given access point, every nearby Android smartphone will send to the Google location service the strength of the signal received from the access point as well as the smartphone’s estimated location.

Given that thousands of smartphones may be passing by the access point during any single day, Google’s location service will have lots of data at its disposal to use in estimating the access point’s position, again by solving trilateration equations.

Thus, the access points help the smartphones determine their locations, and in turn the smartphones help the access points determine their locations!

##### 7.6.2 Satellite Networks

The world of satellite communications has evolved dramatically in the last 10 years. Until 10 years ago, deployed satellite applications primarily used satellites in geostationary orbit (GEO). A geostationary satellite is located roughly 35,000 km above the earth’s equator and rotates with the Earth so that it remains in the same position in the sky relative to observers on Earth. Geostationary satellites have been in use for more than 60 years, for applications including broadcast TV, sensing (e.g., of the weather, atmospheric or surface sensing), and Internet connectivity in areas not served by the terrestrial Internet [Hughes 2025].

The past 10 years, however, have seen a tremendous increase in interest in a different class of satellite networks, known as low earth orbit (LEO) satellites. While the applications remain the same (in particular sensing and Internet connectivity), LEO satellites (LEOs) are generally smaller, less expensive, and positioned much closer to the earth than their GEO counterparts. Located between 500 and 1,200 Km above the surface, LEO satellites thus have much shorter RTTs  ~30 msec  than GEO satellites  ~800 msec  .

As of November

2022, only 6,800 active satellites had been launched in all of history. But in just five years (2019–2024) Starlink alone has launched an equivalent number 6,281 of LEO satellites [space.com 2024]. Today, well over 90% of all satellites launched are LEO satellites. Clearly, there is tremendous recent interest in LEO satellite networks!

LEO satellite network architecture Figure 7.49 shows the principal components of a LEO satellite network:

• LEO satellites. At the top of Figure 7.49, we see the network of orbiting LEO satellites, often referred to as a “constellation” of satellites. Starlink reports more than 6,750 satellites in its constellation; in early 2025 there are approximately 650 LEO satellites in the Oneweb constellation.

Because of their relatively low altitude, LEO satellites are not geostationary but instead are in constant motion with respect to the earth below, travelling at 27,000 km/hr with respect to the ground [Bhattacherjee 2019]. As we’ll see below, these highly mobile network elements take the whole topic of “network mobility” in a whole new direction!

• Satellite links. The coverage area of a satellite’s wireless transmitter/receiver on the earth below is known as its footprint. In the downlink direction, a satellite’s transmissions are broadcast in nature, as they are received by all stations within the footprint. In the uplink direction, transmissions from the various ground stations within the satellite’s footprint are unicast to the satellite—a classical multiple access channel! The footprint of a typical LEO satellite is 15 miles in diameter. A ground station will remain in the footprint of a satellite link’s beam for only 10 minutes or so, until the satellite’s motion takes it out of view of the ground station. You can view the current and changing Starlink and Oneweb constellation footprints (including details for where you are on earth) at https://satellitemap.space/. Satellites may also be directly connected to each other using optical inter-satellite

![](media/page-565-img-01.png)

Figure 7.49 Components of a LEO satellite network links (ISLs), although this type of infrastructure link is not yet widely used in practice.

• Ground stations. On or near the Earth’s surface are the ground stations that transmit and receive datagrams over the satellite link. These ground stations may be connected only to the satellite or may be connected both to the satellite and to the terrestrial Internet, in which case the ground station serves as a gateway between the satellite network and the terrestrial Internet. LEO ground stations often have small dish or flat panel antennas for satellite communication. However, a low-bandwidth SOS emergency texting service via satellite is currently available for some (Apple) cellphones, and the provision of additional 5G-like data services via LEO satellites are under study.

Mobility With LEO satellites whizzing through the air at 27,000 km/hr and with ground stations that may themselves be mobile on trucks, boats or airplanes, LEOS constellations are wireless networks with extreme mobility! In contrast to WiFi and 5G networks, however, it is the LEO network infrastructure (satellites), not the user device, that is the primary source of “mobility.” Since a ground station remains attached to a satellite for only 10 minutes or so, ground-station handover between orbiting satellites is a common and important occurrence, as one satellite moves out-of-range of the ground station, while other satellites remain in-range. Recent measurements suggest that satellite handover is much less well-developed than 5G handover, with suspected packet loss occurring during handovers [Kassem 2022]. Also, unlike 5G networks, there is no LEO satellite network standardization body that is similar in spirit to the 3GPP in the cellular network world. As a result, satellite network implementations remain proprietary.

A link in the air or a network in the air?

Figure 7.50 shows two possible approaches towards building satellite networks. The “bent pipe” architecture (Figure 7.50(a)) treats each satellite as a link, with ground stations at each end of each link. An end-to-end path thus

Figure 7.50 Links in the sky or a network in the sky?

![](media/page-566-img-01.png)

consists of a series of single-hop satellite links, with a packet returning to ground from the sky after each hop. Figure 7.50(b) shows the network-in-thesky approach, where inter-satellite links (ISLs) directly connect satellites, and a packet may cross multiple hops among satellites before returning to ground.

Note that because satellites are non-stationary with respect to the ground and with respect to each other, the ISL links in the network-in-the-sky are dynamically changing, making routing in LEOS networks a challenging problem. For a recent introduction and overview of LEOS networks, see [Bhattacherjee 2019;

Al Homssi 2022; Kassem 2022].

##### 7.6.3 Internet of Things (IoT) networks

The Internet of Things (IoT) [Manyika 2013] is about connecting devices, which are often small and energy-constrained, with computation to sense, monitor, report, and control phenomena in the physical world. Myriad IoT applications in multiple areas abound, including but not limited to (i) manufacturing, where physical characteristics such as pressure, vibration, temperature, humidity, switch settings, and gauge levels are monitored, often with actions then taken; (ii) logistics and supply chains, where asset and transport conditions are monitored and tracked; (iii) agriculture and the environment, where rainfall, temperature, wind, humidity, animal tracking/health, and soil conditions are monitored and resources deployed as a result; (iv) smart cities, where the sound, air, water, weather, lighting, traffic, and crowds, are measured and transportation systems and services are monitored, with services activated and deactivated in response; and (v) personal health monitoring and care. Some have characterized IoT’s impact as being so pervasive and so profound as to constitute a fourth industrial revolution, or “Industry 4.0” [Schwab 2016].

With more than three times as many connected IoT devices deployed than PCs, laptops, tablets, and cellphones combined by the end of this decade [Statista IoT 2025], IoT is on pace to soon become a $300 billion market [Schwab 2016].

With so many different applications with so many different requirements, and such a large potential market, it’s not surprising that there are many different competing technologies angling to provide networked services for IoT. Our modest goal here is to provide an overview of these IoT wireless network technologies, several of which we have already learned about earlier in this chapter, and to provide pointers for additional reading.

Figure 7.51, adapted from [Ahmad 2019], provides a three-faceted characterization of IoT networking technologies, illustrating the extent to which a particular technology emphasizes area coverage, energy consumption, and/or high data rates. Each of the technologies shown in Figure 7.51 emphasizes two of these three characteristics, but none emphasize all three. This suggests that rather than a winner-take-all outcome in IoT networking, we’re likely to see different solutions adopted in practice, depending on the context.

• Emphasizing low energy and low data rate. IEEE 802.11ah, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) and Zigbee are three wireless IoT technologies designed for short-range coverage. IEEE 802.11ah is a “flavor” of WiFi, inheriting much of WiFi’s architecture, including the BSS structure, the notion of channels, and a stripped-down 802.11 frame format. IEEE 802.11ah provides data rates of 100’s kbps to ~5 – 10 Mbps. Operating in the 900 MHz unlicensed band and with relays, these networks can span up to a kilometer in practice. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) [Sauter 2021] is a significant expansion of the original Bluetooth standard to support IoT devices. We learned about Bluetooth networks earlier in Section 7.6.1 and in Section 7.3.6 we learned that BLE (like LoRa Class A, and 4G LTE Narrowband IoT) supports device-initiated wake-and-send transmission by the IoT device.

![](media/page-568-img-01.png)

Figure 7.51 IoT communication technologies and their emphases

Introduced in the late 1990s, Zigbee [Gomez 2010] is one of the earliest IoT networking technologies. It is built on the physical and MAC layers of the IEEE 802.15.4 standard for low-rate wireless personal area networks.

• Emphasizing low energy and wider area coverage. LoRaWAN [Jouhari 2023] (Long Range Wide Area Network) is standardized by International Telecommunication Union (ITU). We covered LoRaWAN’s energy saving mechanisms for Class A devices [Semtech 2019a] in Section 7.3.6; Class B device operation is covered in [Semtech 2019b]. LoRaWAN is a networkwide (as opposed to a link-layer) standard, with servers, gateways, and IoT devices operating with data rate ranging from 0.3 kbit/s to 50 kbit/s per channel in the 902 − 928 MHz unlicensed band. LoRaWAN networks span wide areas using a star-of-star network topology, with a LoRaWAN gateway serving as a coordinating central node in each edgestar network. 4G Narrowband Internet of Things (NB-IoT) [Vaezi 2022] is a 3GPP 4G standard that naturally contains many of the architectural features of the 4G RAN, including base stations, user devices, downlink OFDM and uplink single-carrier FDMA—all of which we studied earlier in  Section 7.3.NB-IoT also supports device-initiated wake-and-send transmission by the IoT device that we encountered in Section 7.6.1.

With 200 kHz channel bandwidths, LTE NB-IoT data rates are limited to approximately 250 Kbps.

• Emphasizing wider area coverage and higher data rates. Long Term Evolution for Machines (LTE-M) is a second, more fully functional 3GPP LTE standard aimed at IoT applications. It supports device mobility among base stations and has channel bandwidths that are 5 times larger than LTE NB-IoT. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), which works with the 3GPP to set the vision for mobile cellular network standards, notes that for 5G, while “initial standards and launches have mostly focused on enhanced Mobile Broadband, 5G is expected to increasingly enable new business models and countless new use cases, in particular those of massive Machine Type Communications and Ultra-reliable and Low Latency Communications.” These two latter broad categories of communication applications include IoT. Thus, while 5G standards and deployments have focused primarily on Mobile Broadband to date, work on supporting IoT within the 5G standard is well underway [Vaezi 2022; 3GPP TS 38.300 2024].

#### 7.7 Summary

Wireless mobile networks first revolutionized telephony and are having an increasingly profound impact in the world of computer networks as well.

With already more than five times as many Internet-connected wireless subscribers as wired subscribers, and with their anytime, anywhere, untethered access into the global network infrastructure, wireless networks are providing nearly ubiquitous wireless Internet connectivity and have enabled an exciting new set of mobile, location-dependent services. Given the importance of wireless and mobile networks, we’ve devoted an entire chapter (this chapter) to this topic.

We began this chapter with an introduction to wireless and mobile networks and then embarked on a bottom-up study of their principles and practice.

In spite of our strong preference for a top-down pedagogical approach, we felt that an early mastery of the underlying radio channel was needed to understand just about every other aspect of wireless networking. Thus, we began our in-depth study of wireless and mobile networks in Section 7.2 with a study of the unique characteristics of a radio channel, and then learned how bits are coded into symbols and then waveforms that are modulated, transmitted, and received over that channel. In Section 7.3 we then turned our attention to wireless access networks, covering techniques for sharing the radio channel, network discovery and device attachment, frame transmission scheduling, and energy conservation. Throughout Section 7.3, we used WiFi and 5G networks to illustrate how the principles we’ve learned are put into practice. In Section 7.4 we then covered the mobile Core network, a key architectural component of cellular networks that provides support for global identity, mobility, and service subscription—services not typically found in the traditional wired Internet. Mobility is such a unique feature of wireless networks, that we devoted an entire section (7.5) to the topic. While we have focused primarily on 5G and WiFi networks throughout this chapter, we briefly covered three other important wireless network architectures—Bluetooth, satellite and IoT wireless networks—in Section 7.6.

Although we’ve devoted an entire chapter to the study of wireless and mobile networks, an entire book (or more!) would be required to fully explore this exciting and rapidly expanding field. A full course could be taught on this topic alone—and such a course is indeed taught by one of the co-authors [Kurose 2025]. We encourage you to delve more deeply into this field by consulting the many resources noted in this chapter.
